docs.title: vem-project
docs.text:
Work in progress

This template is being tested and isn't ready for real projects yet. Things may change without notice. Please report problems in the template's issue tracker.

One-line description of what this tool does for volume EM / CLEM data.

  • Getting started: install it and run the example.
  • Usage: the command line, Python and the container.
  • API reference: every public function, from the docstrings.
  • Development: how to contribute.

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text: Report bugs in the issue tracker, and ask questions on the image.sc forum.

docs.title: Citing
docs.text: Please cite the version you used: see CITATION.cff in the repository, or GitHub's Cite this repository button.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
The scientific and analysis choices made in this project, and why: methods, thresholds, parameters and their defaults, what is excluded, and how results are reported. Code shows what was done; this page records why, so the reasoning survives for reviewers, for the methods section of a paper, and for whoever works on the project next.

When to add an entry: whenever a choice could change the results. Add it in the same pull request as the change. Newest first. Don't edit old entries when you change your mind: add a new one that replaces them, and say so.

How: copy the template below. The reasons must be the researchers' own; an AI assistant can draft the entry but shouldn't invent the reasoning.

docs.title: 2026-10-29: Report object volumes in physical units
docs.text:
• Decision: measure reports each object's volume in cubic units of the image's own voxel size (e.g. nm³), not as a voxel count.
  • Why: volume EM voxels are often anisotropic (e.g. 8 nm in-plane, 16 nm between slices), so voxel counts can't be compared between datasets acquired at different settings.
  • Alternatives considered: voxel counts (rejected: not comparable); converting everything to µm³ (deferred: units are kept as acquired, to avoid rounding very small objects).
  • Effect on results: none yet; this is the template's example.
  • Decided by: the template authors. Replace this example entry with your project's first decision.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
Contributions are welcome. The full guide is CONTRIBUTING.md in the repository. In short:

  1. Work on a branch, never on main.
  2. Make small commits with Conventional Commit messages.
  3. Add tests, and update the docs and CHANGELOG.md.
  4. Open a pull request. It's reviewed (by a colleague where possible, or by yourself with the self-review checklist in REVIEWING.md) and merged.

Set up a development environment:

git clone https://github.com/ccp-volume-em/vem-project.git
cd vem-project
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install -e ".[dev]"
pytest

Preview this documentation with mkdocs serve.

This project follows the CCP-volumeEM good practice guide, summarised in the repository's guidance/ folder.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
You need Python 3.11 or newer. Use a virtual environment, so this project's packages don't interfere with others:

python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate        # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
python -m pip install "vem-project @ git+https://github.com/ccp-volume-em/vem-project"

Check it worked:

vem-project --version

docs.title: Try it on example data
docs.text:
From a copy of the repository, make a small synthetic label volume and measure the objects in it:

python examples/make_example_data.py
vem-project measure examples/params.yml

The first command writes data/example_labels.ome.zarr: two box-shaped objects with 8 × 8 × 16 nm voxels. The second measures them and writes:

  • results/example/object_volumes.csv: the volume of each object in nm³;
  • results/example/provenance.json: the software version, parameters and inputs that produced it.

Object 1 is 8 × 20 × 20 voxels of 1,024 nm³ each, so its volume should be 3,276,800 nm³.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
Generated from the docstrings in the code.

Read and write volumes as OME-Zarr, keeping their physical metadata.

OME-Zarr (also called NGFF) is the community format for large bioimaging data. Reading is lazy: you get a dask array, and voxels are only loaded from disk when a calculation needs them, so volumes larger than memory still work.

Measurements on segmented volumes, in physical units.

Record how an output was produced, so results can be traced and reproduced.

A provenance file sits next to each output and records the software version, the parameters and the inputs. For sharing complete datasets, the CCP-volumeEM guide recommends packaging this information as an RO-Crate (https://www.researchobject.org/ro-crate/); this simple JSON record is a starting point that can be converted later.

docs.title: Volume dataclass
docs.text:
Image or label data together with the metadata needed to interpret it.

Keeping voxel size and units next to the data means measurements can be reported in physical units, and the metadata is not lost when results are written back out.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data Array or ndarray

Voxel values, with axes in the order given by dims.

required dims tuple of str

Axis names, e.g. ("z", "y", "x").

required voxel_size dict of str to float

Size of one voxel along each spatial axis, in unit.

required unit str

Physical unit of voxel_size, as an OME-Zarr unit name such as "nanometer".

'nanometer' name str

Short name stored in the OME-Zarr metadata.

'image'

docs.title: read_ome_zarr(path, level=0)
docs.text:
Open one resolution level of an OME-Zarr image without loading it.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default path str or Path

Local path or URL of the .ome.zarr store.

required level int

Pyramid level, where 0 is full resolution and higher levels are progressively downsampled.

0

Returns:

Type Description Volume

Lazy (dask) data with the voxel size and unit of that level.

docs.title: write_ome_zarr(volume, path, scale_factors=None, labels=False)
docs.text:
Write a volume as OME-Zarr with a multiscale pyramid.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default volume Volume

Data and metadata to write.

required path str or Path

Destination .ome.zarr path. It must not already exist.

required scale_factors list of int

Downsampling factor of each extra pyramid level relative to full resolution, e.g. [2, 4]. By default one level per halving until the image is small.

None labels bool

Set to True for segmentations, so downsampling keeps label values rather than averaging them into values that are not labels.

False

docs.title: object_volumes(labels)
docs.text:
Physical volume of every labelled object.

Works chunk by chunk on dask arrays, so the label image never has to fit in memory.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default labels Volume

Integer label image where 0 is background and each other value is one object. Must have z, y and x voxel sizes.

required

Returns:

Type Description dict of int to float

Object label mapped to its volume in cubic labels.unit, e.g. nm³ for "nanometer". Background (0) is not included.

Examples:

>>> import numpy as np
>>> cube = np.zeros((4, 4, 4), dtype=np.uint8)
>>> cube[:2, :2, :2] = 1
>>> object_volumes(Volume(cube, ("z", "y", "x"), {"z": 10, "y": 5, "x": 5}))
{1: 2000.0}

docs.title: write_provenance(path, parameters, inputs, outputs)
docs.text:
Write a JSON provenance record and return its contents.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default path str or Path

Where to write the record, usually next to the outputs.

required parameters dict

Every parameter that affects the result.

required inputs list of str or pathlib.Path

Files or folders read and written.

required outputs list of str or pathlib.Path

Files or folders read and written.

required

Returns:

Type Description dict

The record that was written.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    params[/"params.yml"/] --> measure
    labels[("labels<br>OME-Zarr")] -->|lazy read, with voxel size| measure["vem-project measure"]
    measure --> csv[/"object_volumes.csv<br>(physical units)"/]
    measure --> prov[/"provenance.json"/]

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
Write a parameter file. Paths are relative to the file:

labels: ../data/my_labels.ome.zarr  # integer label image, OME-Zarr
level: 0                            # pyramid level; 0 = full resolution
output_dir: ../results/my_run

Then run:

vem-project measure params.yml

Keeping the parameters in a file means a run can be repeated exactly, and works the same on a laptop and in an HPC batch job.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
from vem_project.io import read_ome_zarr
from vem_project.measure import object_volumes

labels = read_ome_zarr("data/my_labels.ome.zarr")  # lazy: nothing loaded yet
print(labels.voxel_size, labels.unit)
volumes = object_volumes(labels)  # processed chunk by chunk

docs.title: Container
docs.text:
docker build -t vem-project .
docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
    -v /path/to/project:/data \
    vem-project measure /data/params.yml

-v makes your project folder visible inside the container at /data; --user makes the output files belong to you.

On an HPC cluster with Apptainer, once an image is published:

apptainer pull vem-project.sif docker://ghcr.io/ccp-volume-em/vem-project:v0.1.0
apptainer run --bind /path/to/project:/data vem-project.sif measure /data/params.yml
